title: The pseudoinverse
objectives: Build $\mathbf{A}^+$ from the SVD and use it for least squares when $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}$ is singular.

screens.title: When the normal equations fail
screens.prose: Least squares from lesson 10 solves $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$. Form both sides for this $\mathbf{X}$. $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} = (11, 11)$.
screens.question: Why can we not solve the normal equations?

options.text: $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular: its two equations, $14\beta_1 + 14\beta_2 = 11$, are the same
$\mathbf{y}$ is not in the column space of $\mathbf{X}$
options.why: It is not, which is why this is least squares. The normal equations are built for that case. The fault is in $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$.
Every pair with $\beta_1 + \beta_2 = \tfrac{11}{14}$ is a best fit. There are too many, not too few.
Tall matrices are the normal case in least squares. A tall matrix with independent columns gives an invertible $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$.

The rows are equal, so the determinant is $14 \times 14 - 14 \times 14 = 0$.
A singular matrix has no inverse, so $(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}$ does not exist.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the determinant of $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$.

explain.text: The columns of $\mathbf{X}$ are dependent, so $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular and the normal equations give one equation for two unknowns. NumPy's `inv` returns a matrix of `nan` here, or raises an error. We need a rule that picks one answer.

The eigenvalues are 28 and 0 (trace 28, determinant 0).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the square root of the eigenvalue 28.

byKey.half: 3.7417 is $\sqrt{14}$, the root of one entry of $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$. The eigenvalue is 28.
byKey.trace: 14 is a diagonal entry. The eigenvalue is the trace, 28.

explain.text: $\mathbf{X} = \sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1\mathbf{v}_1^T$ with $\mathbf{u}_1 = (1, 2, 3)/\sqrt{14}$ and $\mathbf{v}_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2$. A matrix is inverted by inverting each stretch. The stretch $\sigma_1$ inverts to $1/\sigma_1 = 0.189$; the zero has no inverse.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def pinv_svd(A, tol=1e-10):
    """Pseudoinverse from the SVD. A singular value below
    tol times the largest one is treated as zero."""
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
    keep = s > tol * s.max()
    s_inv = np.zeros_like(s)
    s_inv[keep] = 1.0 / s[keep]
    return Vt.T @ np.diag(s_inv) @ U.T

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def pinv_svd(A, tol=1e-10):
    """Pseudoinverse from the SVD. A singular value below
    tol times the largest one is treated as zero."""
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
    keep = s > tol * s.max()
    s_inv = np.zeros_like(s)
    s_inv[keep] = 1.0 / s[keep]
    return Vt.T @ np.diag(s_inv) @ U.T


def hedge_min_norm(X, y, tol=1e-6):
    """Least-squares hedge ratios of smallest length."""
    return pinv_svd(X, tol) @ np.asarray(y, dtype=float)

screens.title: Hedging with a redundant instrument
screens.prose: A desk hedges a book with three futures, and $F_3$ is always $F_1 + F_2$. The table gives each future's P&L per unit in four scenarios, and the book's P&L in £k. Each hedge below fits the book exactly. Trading cost grows with the square of each position.
screens.question: Which hedge $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$ has the smallest sum of squared positions?

options.why: You chose the hedge that skips a future. It has squares summing to 26, the largest of the four.
You minimised the sum of sizes, 5 against 6. The squares sum to 17, which is more than 14.
This fits too, but its squares sum to 17.

hints.text: All four hedges differ by multiples of $(1, 1, -1)$, which nets to nothing because $F_3 = F_1 + F_2$.
The shortest one is perpendicular to $(1, 1, -1)$, so $b_1 + b_2 = b_3$.
Only $(1, 2, 3)$ has $b_1 + b_2 = b_3$. It is $\mathbf{X}^+\mathbf{y}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the squares of each hedge, or find the one with $b_1 + b_2 = b_3$.

byKey.skip: Skipping a future does not make a hedge small. Add the squares: $1 + 0 + 25 = 26$.
byKey.gross: Gross size is $|b_1| + |b_2| + |b_3|$. We are asked for squares.

explain.text: Every hedge in the line $(1, 2, 3) + t(1, 1, -1)$ hedges equally well, because $F_1 + F_2 - F_3$ is always zero. The pseudoinverse picks $t = 0$, the smallest total square, so it trades the least when cost grows with size squared. It also stays stable when the data change a little.

ideas: $\mathbf{A}^+ = \mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^+\mathbf{U}^T$: invert each nonzero singular value and leave each zero at zero. $\mathbf{A}^+\mathbf{b}$ is the least-squares solution of smallest length.

With independent columns $\mathbf{A}^+ = (\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^T$, and for a square invertible matrix $\mathbf{A}^+ = \mathbf{A}^{-1}$. $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^+$ projects onto the column space and $\mathbf{A}^+\mathbf{A}$ onto the row space.
A tiny singular value has a huge reciprocal. Treat anything below $\text{tol} \times \sigma_1$ as zero, and never invert $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ for near-duplicate columns.
